constitutional surface uses version labels is the
[§2 Specification surface rule](#specification-surface-rule); shared
realisation surfaces should likewise describe current truth by role,
boundary and status rather than by release-line version labels. Release criteria, immutable
release-cut publication, selector advancement and the process for cutting a
release belong to [RELEASE §2 to §8](RELEASE.md#2-release-identities)
(provenance rc.2 RELEASE_METHOD #release-identities, #phases, #naming,
#coordinated-release-matched-asset-cohorts).

Successor baseline conservation is
[RELEASE §9](RELEASE.md#9-successor-baseline-conservation-stdo-up-015)
(P3, P6; provenance rc.2 RELEASE_METHOD
#successor-baseline-conservation-stdo-up-015).

Layer and release separation holds
([AXIOMATIC_CALCULUS §7](AXIOMATIC_CALCULUS.md#ac-020-layer-and-release-separation)):
a calculus, its interpretation of a subject and its carrier encoding keep
independent content identities, judgments, supersession relations and
proof obligations, and none is automatically an independently released
product. One constitutional surface and its version boundary for a project
are
[PRODUCT_DEFINITION §11](PRODUCT_DEFINITION.md#11-one-constitutional-surface-and-version-boundary).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/6. Lineage and release/Shared method adoption and propagation (STDO-UP-012)
segments.text:
### Shared method adoption and propagation (STDO-UP-012)

A reusable change to this method keeps one authority relation from the
evidence that prompts it to the consumer that realises it (P6, P3;
provenance rc.2 POSTING_GUIDE
#shared-method-adoption-and-propagation-stdo-up-012):

```text
incident or review evidence
  -> shared-method intake
  -> one owning standard
  -> consistency and independent review
  -> human-authority acceptance
  -> one complete released STDO version
  -> explicit consumer selection
  -> consumer-owned realisation and evidence
```

The chain states authority causality. It prescribes no intake workflow and
no artifact set (P2). An executable tool, runtime, carrier schema or
assurance implementation cannot enter the method merely because it
accompanies a method lesson; it requires its own Product authorisation
(P6). Other standards consume admitted law by reference (P3, P6), and a
consumer selects a complete released version rather than mixing members from different cuts (P3;
the release version boundary above,
[PRODUCT_DEFINITION §4](PRODUCT_DEFINITION.md#4-shared-installed-release-basis-and-toolchain-manager)).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration
segments.text: ## 7. Migration

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Core interface migration
segments.text:
### Core interface migration

Core interface changes are not ordinary local patches. Where a change
alters a load-bearing contract, carrier, resolver, provider, projection
law, closure law or other shared interface that multiple surfaces depend
on, the work is handled as a constitutional migration, not as incremental
patching (P3, P6; rc.2 #core-interface-migration-rule). The governing rule:
change the authoritative core contract first; ban bridge code for that
contract family as an authoritative surface; audit every producer and every
consumer of the impacted interface; migrate each producer and consumer to
the new contract; chase every downstream effect until no superseded closure
law remains; run complete migration-closure proof only after the migration
wave is complete, bounded product-slice proof remaining governed by the
path-relative promotion rule below.

The rule exists because partial interface migration creates recurring
drift: one producer writes the new contract while another still writes the
old; runtime reads one carrier while reporting or topology reads another;
compatibility aliases silently remain authoritative; projections become a
second truth surface; tests go green while the architecture remains split.
Declaring such a state complete is forbidden.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Constitutional migration options
segments.text:
### Constitutional migration options

Core interface and major implementation replacement work has two lawful
constitutional strategies (P3, P6; rc.2 #constitutional-migration-options).
Inside-out hard-break migration applies when the project remains on the
same implementation line and the authoritative source truth is being
replaced in place; the work proceeds from the source carrier outward
through a sequence of deliberate breaks and repairs. Fundamental
re-adoption migration applies when the rewrite is major and the project is
intentionally re-deriving itself on a materially different implementation
basis, such as a new runtime model, carrier model, type system, execution
substrate or realisation tree; the prior implementation is moved sideways
and treated as reference material, not live authority.

Where bounded evolution and fundamental re-adoption are both lawful and
feasible, and a working predecessor can reach the admitted product outcome
without retaining competing or ambiguous authority, evolution on the
supported product path is the rebuttable selection presumption. This does
not require continuing an unsafe or constitutionally inadmissible
predecessor path; it conserves accepted predecessor semantics and product
feedback, and it does not require preserving an internal implementation or
public mechanism that product authority explicitly supersedes. When bounded
evolution includes a core-interface migration, it uses the inside-out
hard-break strategy; bounded evolution is a strategy-selection presumption,
not a third strategy.

Fundamental re-adoption requires explicit selection by the human authority
owning the affected product boundary. The selection compares re-adoption
with bounded evolution across product value, feedback latency, authority
risk, reversibility, total cost and retained predecessor semantics, and
states a bounded abort or re-entry condition. Implementation scale or
architectural preference alone does not select re-adoption (P6, P2).

Both strategies share these non-negotiable rules: no proxy interface
partial implementation stands in for the new contract in any acceptance
path; no bridge or fallback path remains silently authoritative; promotion
of an affected product outcome requires one unambiguous authoritative path
for that outcome; competing or ambiguous executable authority on the
promoted acceptance path blocks that outcome; residual material from the
superseded interface family outside the promoted path may be deferred only
when it is explicitly non-authoritative for the promoted outcome or governs
an explicitly specified, disjoint product or compatibility scope with
deterministic routing, cannot falsify current or retained product claims,
and retains a bounded migration, qualification or release disposition;
tests are leak detectors and proof surfaces, not the migration plan.

For this rule the affected acceptance path is the full causal closure of
the outcome: every admitted entrypoint, producer, consumer, resolver,
fallback, shared state surface, event, projection and proof surface capable
of changing, interpreting or closing the outcome. Singular authority means
one governing authority across that closure, not one selected successful
trace. If the same request, fact, identity, state or projection is
admissible to old and new authority, authority is competing and promotion
blocks (P3).

Product-slice promotion and complete migration closure are distinct claims.
An intermediate product outcome may be promoted while its enclosing
migration remains open only when the outcome's acceptance path has singular
authority and the residual implementation satisfies the deferment rule
above. That promotion neither closes the migration nor waives its final
retirement criteria. The slice's identity and acceptance criteria derive
from the product plus every causally applicable live requirement, accepted
design relation and retained predecessor claim; ticket or review wording
cannot narrow that authority away. Active migration status does not renew
an accepted slice's exhausted growth authority: work that only discharges
already admitted removal, demotion and migration-closure proof obligations
may continue within that existing bound without claiming further product
progress; further material producer or consumer growth requires another
still-live basis admitted under §3, and ticket activity alone is not that
basis.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/What counts as a core interface
segments.text:
### What counts as a core interface

A core interface is any shared contract or carrier that materially governs
runtime closure, reporting or status truth, topology or frame progression,
proof or qualification outcome, event or projection semantics, identity or
binding resolution, or provider or resolver behaviour. If changing the
interface can alter how multiple surfaces decide what is true now, it is a
core interface change (P3; rc.2 #what-counts-as-a-core-interface).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Required migration protocol
segments.text:
### Required migration protocol

Every core interface migration explicitly declares: the exact affected
migration scope; every explicitly excluded or disjoint product or
compatibility scope and its deterministic routing relation; the new
authoritative contract; the superseded contract or surface; the
authoritative closure law for the new contract; the full set of producers
of the old and new contract; the full set of consumers of the old and new
contract; and every projection, report, status surface and proof surface
that derives from it. Every old path is then classified as `remove`,
`replace`, `re-authorize` or `temporary scaffolding`. Temporary scaffolding
is lawful only if it is explicitly non-authoritative and scheduled for
removal before closure (P6, P4b; rc.2 #required-migration-protocol).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Bridge prohibition
segments.text:
### Bridge prohibition

For a core interface migration: no compatibility alias remains
authoritative; no fallback identity law remains as silent runtime
behaviour; no bridge path participates in acceptance as if it were the new
contract; no old reader or writer remains authoritative for the promoted
outcome once the new contract governs that outcome; no proxy or partial
implementation of the new interface stands between old and new truth as if
it were completion. The only lawful exception is an explicit compatibility
feature retained as part of the live product, whose compatibility path is
intentionally specified, explicitly bounded, and clearly identified as
compatibility rather than current native truth (P3, P6; rc.2
#bridge-prohibition).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Projection discipline
segments.text:
### Projection discipline

Projections, reports, status views and topology views may reflect the
authoritative carrier; they do not become a second closure surface (P6,
P1; rc.2 #projection-discipline). If runtime, reporting, topology and proof
can disagree about closure because they consume different carriers or
different closure laws, the migration is incomplete; if a projection can
independently close while the authoritative carrier is still open, the
migration is incomplete; if the authoritative carrier can close while a
projection still depends on an older law, the migration is incomplete.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Inside-out first sequencing
segments.text:
### Inside-out first sequencing

Inside-out hard-break migrations proceed from the new authoritative source
carrier outward (P4b, P6; rc.2 #inside-out-first-sequencing). The full
best-guess interface family is discovered before proof is used as closure
evidence, including producers, consumers, projections, prompts, reports,
wrappers, replay paths, ingest paths, bootstrap paths and proof surfaces.
Authoritative producer and source-carrier work comes before downstream
consumer, projection, prompt, dossier, report or review-surface hardening.
Downstream exploration may exist only as isolated non-authoritative work
and does not land in public runtime, projection, prompt, report or proof
entry points until the source carrier is published and admitted. A
downstream projection ticket does not close while the source-carrier
ticket it depends on is still open. Dependency direction reflects this
order explicitly so the ticket set exposes the migration wave from source
truth to downstream read models.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Hard-break discipline
segments.text:
### Hard-break discipline

Inside-out migration is a hard-break sequence over one interface family.
The migration wave is the ordered set of those breaks; it is not a separate
mode that permits competing or ambiguous dual truth over the same request,
fact, identity, state or projection. Explicitly specified, deterministically
routed, non-overlapping product or compatibility scopes may coexist while
the enclosing migration remains open (P3; rc.2 #hard-break-discipline).

For each break: publish or admit the new deepest authoritative source
carrier; deliberately sever one old authoritative seam; keep that seam
broken; repair outward from source truth to consumers, then projections,
then prompts and reports, then proof surfaces; run negative proof that the
severed seam is rejected rather than merely unused. During the sequence,
tests may discover missed interfaces but do not replace the required
interface inventory; newly discovered affected interfaces remain part of
the same migration wave unless the work is explicitly repriced upward;
re-enabling the old seam through wrappers, fallbacks, projections or prompt
paths is a migration defect.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Proof-last rule
segments.text:
### Proof-last rule

Complete migration-closure proof is not valid while producers and
consumers are split across old and new contracts. Bounded product-slice
proof may establish only the exact intermediate outcome permitted by the
path-relative promotion rule; it cannot establish migration closure (P6;
rc.2 #proof-last-rule-for-core-interface-changes). Tests that pass only
because bridge-state semantics remain alive do not count as closure proof;
green local tests do not overrule a split architecture; migration-closure
proof belongs after migration, not during a partially migrated state;
per-break proof shows the severed old seam is rejected or fails closed
before downstream hardening can count as progress.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Closure criterion
segments.text:
### Closure criterion

A core interface migration is complete across its declared affected scope
only when every authoritative producer writes the new contract; every
authoritative consumer reads the new contract; superseded authoritative
paths are retired unless justified for a distinct supported responsibility
under the retention relation below; projections are downstream of the same
authoritative truth rather than competing truth surfaces; runtime,
reporting, topology and proof share one closure law; and no temporary
scaffolding remains in the acceptance path. Until those conditions hold the
work remains an active migration wave, not a completed refactor (P3, P6;
rc.2 #closure-criterion).

Retention bears the burden. Each retained superseded mechanism identifies a
current supported obligation, owner, purpose, execution scope and material
cost. Temporary compatibility or comparison work has an expiry or removal
trigger; existing tests, an oracle label or nominal demotion do not justify
duplicate production responsibility. A required cold reconstruction route
or independent test oracle may serve an enduring distinct obligation
without an invented expiry. Where an obligation survives replacement, its
surviving owner is identified; where it has no governing basis, no
replacement guard is required. Retirement inside a closed affected cone
does not await unrelated whole-product closure (P2).

An accepted intermediate product slice within the wave names the slice it
closes and keeps the enclosing migration visibly open; it does not project
slice acceptance as migration, qualification or release closure.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Fundamental migration
segments.text:
### Fundamental migration

A fundamental migration is a constitutional reset, not an in-place
refactor. It applies when a project intentionally abandons a prior
constitutional shape and re-derives itself on a new branch, version line or
methodology basis (P3, P6; rc.2 #fundamental-migration-rule). In that case:
inherited constitutional documents from the prior line become migration
source material, not live authority in the new line; it is lawful to zero
inherited constitutional surfaces on the migration line and rebuild them
from first principles; nothing carries forward by default, and every
retained statement, requirement, design choice or guide rule must be
explicitly re-adopted; every carry-forward is intentional and should land in the
correct layer, goals, intent, product, requirements, design, guide or template; old
design and code may be used as reference implementations but do not govern
the new constitutional surface unless explicitly re-derived and re-adopted;
absence from the new constitutional surface means not yet adopted and
carries no automatic authority from the prior line; the prior
implementation may be moved sideways as a reference line, and that sideways
line has no live implementation authority in the new line; every inherited
module, interface, carrier, projection and proof surface is explicitly
classified before reuse.

The required implementation classifications are `carry_across` (the module
remains materially the same and is intentionally re-adopted into the new
line), `redundant` (no longer needed in the new line) and `rewrite`
(still needed but rebuilt under the new requirements and design).
Unclassified inherited implementation is a defect. The purpose is to
prevent accidental law from leaking through migration by mere inheritance:
fundamental migration is controlled adoption, not passive preservation.

Performing a fundamental migration: declare the migration line and treat
the prior line as source material; establish fresh constitutional surfaces
for method, goals, intent, product, requirements and design; move the
prior implementation sideways if needed so it cannot continue as ambient
live authority; classify inherited constitutional material as adopted,
superseded, deferred or orphaned; classify inherited implementation
material as `carry_across`, `redundant` or `rewrite`; copy forward only
what is intentionally retained; re-derive downstream design and code from
the new constitutional surfaces, not from ambient precedent. In a
fundamental migration `carry_across` does not mean automatic copy-forward
but explicit re-adoption under the new line; direct runtime, projection,
prompt, proof or review dependence on the sideways implementation line is
bridge debt; proxy interfaces that partially imitate the target line while
still depending on the sideways line are not lawful closure. This is a
lawful form of supersession, not a violation of live surface immutability
(§2), because the new line creates a new constitutional surface rather than
silently mutating the old one.

The four classes of inherited constitutional material record the
adoption decision the new line takes on each inherited statement. For an
inherited requirement, the legacy classifications of
[§2 Requirement categories and classification](#requirement-categories-and-classification)
record a different thing: the standing of a requirement that is in the
live surface. The two relate as follows, and are not one classification:
- an adopted requirement enters the live surface as Active, or as Deferred
  when it is adopted as an explicitly not-yet-operative obligation;
- a requirement whose adoption is deferred is not in the live surface: it
  has no legacy classification and no authority until it is adopted,
  because absence from the new surface means "not yet adopted";
- a superseded or orphaned inherited requirement takes Superseded or
  Orphaned, with that table's meanings.

For other inherited
constitutional material the classes keep their names and the steps
above. They are declared states of the new line's surfaces and, as §2
states, none of them is or supplies the
[RELEASE §9](RELEASE.md#9-successor-baseline-conservation-stdo-up-015)
disposition of a predecessor claim (P3, P6). Purpose and material
relation: an inherited requirement in a migration falls under both this
step and the legacy classification rule, and stating how the two records
relate leaves no two records of one standing to reconcile (P3).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/7. Migration/Transformation wave
segments.text:
### Transformation wave

Refactor and migration should be understood as a transformation wave over
mutable
implementation surfaces (P3, P6; rc.2 #transformation-wave-rule). While
the wave is in flight: temporary mixed-state implementation may exist only
below the current break boundary and only as explicitly non-authoritative
plumbing; transitional adapters or scaffolds may exist only when they are
named, bounded and outside the acceptance path; refactor state may still
carry traces of the prior operative model, never as competing or ambiguous
dual authority over the same request, fact, identity, state or projection.
Explicitly specified, deterministically routed, non-overlapping product or
compatibility scopes are not competing authority under this rule; they may
coexist while the enclosing migration remains visibly open.

When the wave lands across its declared affected scope: only the new
current operative surface remains live for that scope; prior operative
paths for that scope are erased from the live product; the path taken to
get there survives only in version control, event history and superseded
records; mixed old and new operative models are not a stable end state. The
only lawful exception is an explicit compatibility feature, which is named
as current product behaviour, justified in the specification, bounded in
scope and tested as an intentional feature. Otherwise the correct action is
deletion, not passive preservation.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/8. Bounded execution in this method
segments.text:
## 8. Bounded execution in this method

Construction delegated to a probabilistic or agentic worker is governed as
the step of ACTIVATION: the execution relation from accepted governing
basis through bounded affected relation set, selected computational
relations, delegated execution and decision authority, construction and
self-review, independent live-surface assessment where required, one of
accept, local repair, re-enter or reject, the exact accepted checkpoint,
and the next already-authorised bounded action (ACTIVATION §1, §3, §5 and
§7; provenance rc.2 #agentic-construction-execution-stdo-up-020). The
construction relation that the step serves, from the bound current state
to the destination through a selected strategy, feedback and the distinct
claims of preservation, progress and completion, is
[ACTIVATION §1 Construction relation](ACTIVATION.md#construction-relation);
this member applies it to delivery and correction (§4) and states no
second relation (P6). The
step states its results in the core of
[FOUNDATIONS §4 Results](FOUNDATIONS.md#results) through the refinements
of [ACTIVATION §3](ACTIVATION.md#3-step-results-and-disposition): that a
candidate is available, how each assessment of it came out, and the
decision owner's disposition (`accept`, `local_repair`, `re_enter` or
`reject`) are separate results, so a candidate that is available or
assessed is not thereby accepted (P6). The selected computational relations
are drawn from the computational calculus of the tenant doing the work;
the actors, tools and processes that carry out the step belong to that
tenant's execution environment, and the step's time, spend and other
resource limits are those of its execution binding (§11). The
declared work boundary of a probabilistic unit is FOUNDATIONS §2 (work
boundary) and §3 (P0); the complete enclosing-relation admission of a
material transition and its standing structural qualification are
ACTIVATION §4; proportionality is ACTIVATION §6. This member binds the
generic terms to its own: the selected outcome of a step is the product
outcome, prerequisite or experiment of §3; the owning relations are the
chain's layers; the re-entry conditions are the change classes of §4.

Delivery priority applies the proportionality relation to the current
product outcome, likelihood, impact, reversibility, dependency and the cost
of delayed product feedback. Probability informs lawful priority; it does
not waive authority, integrity, safety, retained release claims or another
hard stop. A probability stated for priority is a quantified claim under
[FOUNDATIONS §4 Quantified assurance](FOUNDATIONS.md#quantified-assurance);
unsupported numeric confidence stays unresolved (P6). The default priority is work that exposes or advances the
smallest supported product path and its highest-value likely failures.
Defensive or prerequisite work that displaces that path identifies the
affected claim, evidence basis, bounded effort, return condition and
expected product consequence. This is a priority relation, not a fixed
global execution sequence or a scheduling runtime (P2, P0; rc.2
#proportional-method-and-delivery-stdo-up-014, delivery paragraphs).

Which frames carry construction, assessment and disposition, and which
consumer receives a step's return, is set by the configuration that
[ACTIVATION §1 Configuration](ACTIVATION.md#configuration) derives from the
task's operations, dependencies, actor capabilities and required
assurance; this member adds no role inventory, coordinator or sequence. A
step's return goes to the consumer the configuration declares. Where the
configuration has a coordinator, the coordinator decides as
[ACTIVATION §1 Configuration](ACTIVATION.md#configuration), Coordination
across tasks, states, within its decision grant, and selects the next
authorised action. The executive configuration, with its Executive,
Worker and Reviewer frames, is one such configuration; the executive
baseline profile owns it, and it governs where it is selected
([EXECUTIVE_BASELINE](EXECUTIVE_BASELINE.md); provenance rc.2
STDO_REFERENCE_FRAME_BASELINE #executive, #worker, #reviewer) (P0, P6).

Delivery is sequenced around the smallest real path from a supported entry
to a material outcome, established early and widened by increments chosen
for consequential uncertainty, interface reach and failure impact; a
passing path establishes only the relations it exercised. This is a
sequencing heuristic for any realisation, not law; the baseline's
steel-thread delivery governs its profile unchanged (P2; provenance rc.2
STDO_REFERENCE_FRAME_BASELINE #steel-thread-delivery; its row is disposed at
that member).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/9. Evidence
segments.text:
## 9. Evidence

The rules that govern how constitutional claims are proved in practice are
tier-1 law: proof target identity and adequacy (EVALUATION §1); semantic,
evidence and projection separation (EVALUATION §2); assurance-boundary
congruence and method qualification (EVALUATION §1, §3, §6 and §7).
Verification layers, the testing strategy taxonomy with fixture and proof
portability, test authority, scenario bundles, installed development proof
and significant path coverage are ASSURANCE §1 to §6 (P6; rc.2
#evidence-rules is the heading over the first three).

For a realisation claim, the evidence that the closure condition of
[TICKETS §7 Condition-based closure and reuse](TICKETS.md#condition-based-closure-and-reuse)
requires includes an authority trace, realisation proof, negative proof
where drift is plausible, and a present-tense statement of the residual
open pressure; this section adds no second closure condition (P6, P4b,
P5; provenance rc.2
authority_compressions/stdo_compressed.md, proof compression, a claim no
rc.2 body states).

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/10. Design records
segments.text:
## 10. Design records

Each ADR explicitly includes `Status:` (`active`, `superseded` or
`retired`); `Implements:` (the requirement identifiers the ADR makes true);
`Derives from:` (the intent identifier or strategy document that motivated
the decision); `Supersedes:` (the prior ADR or doctrine it replaces);
`Superseded by:` (the successor ADR when its status is superseded); and
`Retained special case:` (when earlier behaviour is intentionally retained
as a special case of the current surface) (P6, P4b; rc.2 #adr-conventions).
ADRs are written per decision boundary, not per requirement file; the
boundary is the question "what design choice makes these acceptance
criteria true". If a requirement names an operational mechanism, the ADR
names that mechanism too. If a requirement expands the event taxonomy, the
event-contract ADR is repriced immediately; event semantics do not drift
into a second constitution.

ADRs are append-only history. When a later ADR supersedes one, the earlier
ADR stays in place with `Status: superseded` and `Superseded by:` naming
its successor; a superseded ADR is deleted only when it is explicitly
retired. When the scope of a shared or cross-tenant ADR narrows during
implementation to one tenant, the ADR moves to that tenant's design
surface and the move is recorded in the supersession chain (P4b, P3;
provenance rc.2 `templates/build_tenants/common/design/adrs/README_TEMPLATE.md`
and the variant README template, Boundary rule and Supersession). Purpose
and material relation: these two rules decided ADR lifecycle and location
but were stated only in templates, so they had no member owner; this
section owns them and the templates refer.

ADRs are stored at the design surface that owns the decision; an `adrs/`
subdirectory is the default scaffold, not a mandatory location (P3; rc.2
#adr-folder-convention). Tenant-local build-tenant ADRs go to the
applicable tenant design surface bound by the product definition, by
default `build_tenants/<tenant-path>/design/adrs/`; shared or cross-tenant
ADRs to the applicable common surface, by default
`build_tenants/common/design/adrs/`; non-tenanted or project-local ADRs to
`<governing-design-surface>/adrs/`. In the default scaffold `<tenant-path>`
is one or more path segments beneath `build_tenants/`; both
capability-oriented `<product-family>/<realization-variant>` paths and
single-label `<realization-variant>` paths are lawful, the former is the
recommended default, existing or alternative layouts remain conformant and
need no migration, and in every layout the product's tenant registry entry
records the tenant identity and locations used (PRODUCT_DEFINITION §1).
The governing design surface is the closest design surface whose authority
owns the decision. ADRs are not placed in comments, generated views,
runtime archives or requirement folders. The filename convention is
`ADR-<local-id>-short-slug.md`, the local identifier unique within the
owning `adrs/` directory; numeric identifiers such as `ADR-001-...` are the
default, and namespace-prefixed identifiers such as `ADR-GM-005-...` are
allowed when the owning design surface already uses them. A `REGISTRY.md`
index alongside the ADR files is recommended for tooling and review and is
not required: the constitutional source remains each ADR file, and a
registry is a read model that may drift unless tooling maintains it.

segments.heading: SPEC_METHOD/11. Build-tenant binding
segments.text:
## 11. Build-tenant binding

This section owns the relation between a product's WHAT and the build
tenants that realise it: what a tenant binds, what stays fixed while it
chooses, and what its evidence shows. It applies to every product built
with this method (P2, P1, P6).

Terms used in this section:

- A build tenant is one independent, project-owned HOW realisation of a
  product's WHAT. The build-tenancy context of
  [PRODUCT_DEFINITION §8](PRODUCT_DEFINITION.md#8-what-how-and-work-carriers)
  names it, and the product definition's tenant registry locates each one.
- The requirements calculus of a product is the set of obligations its
  WHAT states, the outcomes it permits, and its rules for refining and
  composing the work that realises it.
- A computational calculus is a declared set of executable operations,
  with the laws by which they compose, the transformations they permit,
  and their effects and resource behaviour, as far as these are material
  to the obligations.
- An execution environment is the concrete means that performs those
  operations: a technology stack; a human process, made of people, roles,
  documents, communication channels and decision procedures; or a
  combination of the two.
- A tenant's build-tenant binding has two parts: its calculus binding,
  from the requirements calculus to its computational calculus, and its
  execution binding, from that computational calculus to its execution
  environment. A tenant's registry entry locates the tenant; it is not the
  binding.
- A generic procedure is a method procedure whose scope is independent of
  the selected execution environment. It and its projections preserve the
  bindings Rule 2 permits: code, an event stream or reconstruction from a
  complete history is required only where the governing obligations or
  the selected execution binding require it, and an adequate human
  process using current records and direct observation is a permitted
  execution binding of a generic procedure that requires none of them
  (P1, P6; law carried from the common binding requirement).
- Author identity and actor identity are as
  [EVALUATION §3](EVALUATION.md#3-independent-assessment) defines them:
  authorship is one condition of an assessment's independence there, and
  an actor's identity is not an authority.
  Operation kind is what an operation does, such as construct, assess,
  relay, record, measure or decide, together with the authority that kind
  of operation requires.

Rules:

1. Realisations of one WHAT. One WHAT is realised by one or more
   independent build tenants, whatever the physical layout. The WHAT is
   constitutional and each tenant's realisation is HOW; a tenant-local
   realisation stays derivative until its governing truth is ratified in
   specification (§2). Each tenant binds the product's requirements
   calculus to a declared computational calculus and binds that calculus
   to a concrete execution environment. Both bindings are that tenant's
   design and realisation: they are declared in its existing design and
   realisation surfaces, chosen under the Design rule (§2) and recorded as
   design decisions (§10), and the method requires no further carrier. The
   tenant owns its binding, its realisation and their evidence; the WHAT
   keeps its meaning (P2, P6).
2. Selection. The execution environment may be a technology stack, a
   human process or a combination. Its selection stays within the
   requirements calculus, including every human decision that calculus
   requires: no choice of environment removes a required human decision or
   a required independent assessment. Author identity, actor identity and
   operation kind stay distinct, and none determines another. Who authored
   a tenant does not select its environment; one actor may perform
   operations of several kinds, each under its own grant; and an actor's
   identity neither decides the kind of an operation nor grants authority
   for it. A person performing an operation does not by that make it human
   adjudication: §5 states the admission that makes an operation human
   adjudication and how a person who decides under policy without it is
   governed. The same holds for every decision the requirements reserve to
   a human: the person the governing authority admits for it takes it, and
   a person's part elsewhere in the process does not (P6, P1).
3. Material content. For the obligations it serves, the binding
   identifies:
   - the operations, each with its inputs, outputs, effects and outcome
     values; each outcome value maps to exactly one core value under
     [FOUNDATIONS §4 Results](FOUNDATIONS.md#results), and an intended
     external effect, one of uncertain completion included, is recorded as
     [ACTIVATION §3 Effects](ACTIVATION.md#effects) states;
   - the composition laws, and the transformations the calculus permits;
   - the resource measures;
   - the operational assumptions on which conformance depends, among them
     those about actors, tools, availability and failure.

   Human effort, elapsed time, communication and machine resources are
   measured where a selected obligation needs them. Each measure states its
   unit and its boundary: what is counted, and where measurement starts and
   stops. A resource claim without its unit or its boundary supports no
   conformance claim. The size of a selected context is measured as
   [ACTIVATION §2](ACTIVATION.md#2-context-construction-under-an-envelope)
   step 3 measures it, against the capacity the binding declares for the
   actor. The law for declaring, measuring and honouring resource limits
   is [ACTIVATION §6 Resource limits](ACTIVATION.md#resource-limits), and
   this rule binds it: the values of a step's time, spend and other
   resource limits, and the units and boundaries the environment can
   measure, are those of the execution binding, stated before the
   activation they limit. Where a configuration states its resource limits
   and its assumptions about failure
   ([ACTIVATION §1 Configuration](ACTIVATION.md#configuration)), it takes
   them from this binding (P0, P2, P5).
4. Conformance evidence. The obligations of the requirements calculus
   decide fitness; the kind of executor alone neither accepts nor rejects a
   realisation. Evidence establishes how the bound realisation satisfies
   the required meaning and constraints, including the applicable
   authority, independence, failure and recovery conditions. Conformance is
   judged under
   [EVALUATION §6](EVALUATION.md#6-conformance-of-realisations), and two
   conforming tenants need not behave identically outside the contract.
   Each assessment returns a core value for its predicate, and the tenant's
   conformance is their
   [conjunction](FOUNDATIONS.md#conjunction-of-results), with the
   obligations of the requirements calculus as its required coverage. A
   convenient stack never weakens an obligation. An execution plan that
   merges two required independent assessments, or substitutes an
   automated result for a required human decision, is a counterexample to
   the obligation it weakens, so the binding's conformance for that
   obligation is `falsified`; in any run under such a plan the lost
   assessment or decision has no applicable closed result. Matching
   outputs, lower cost or a faster run do not discharge the lost
   independence or authority. A claim that a binding preserves categorical
   structure is a further claim: it meets the Formal fragment of
   [FOUNDATIONS §4](FOUNDATIONS.md#4-algebra) and stays distinct from
   conformance on the equivalence ladder of EVALUATION §6 (P6, P1, P4b).
5. Reuse. A computational calculus may be reused across tenants and
   execution environments wherever each binding satisfies its laws, and
   each binding shows that it does. A different language, tool, team or
   person does not by itself require a different calculus: replacing the
   executor of an operation while the calculus's laws hold changes the
   execution binding, not the calculus (P1, P4a).
6. Representation. A representation of the requirements calculus or of a
   binding in a_c, the axiomatic calculus of
   [AXIOMATIC_CALCULUS](AXIOMATIC_CALCULUS.md), prescribes no executor and
   does not establish execution conformance by structural validation alone
   ([AC-018](AXIOMATIC_CALCULUS.md#ac-018-structural-and-semantic-separation)).
   An a_c model of a human process that passes structural validation
   neither selects an automated executor nor shows that the process meets
   its requirements; execution conformance needs its own evidence under
   rule 4 (P1, P6).
7. Three accounts. The algorithmic, informational and computational
   accounts of a construction, which
   [FOUNDATIONS §2 Accounts of a construction](FOUNDATIONS.md#accounts-of-a-construction)
   defines, apply across the binding, from the requirements calculus
   through the computational calculus to the execution environment. The
   binding keeps the three accounts apart. A mapping from one account to
   another is a transformation: what it preserves, the law that licenses
   it, and whether it is exact or approximate with its adequacy relation
   and end-to-end bound, are stated and discharged under
   [ACTIVATION §4 Refinement](ACTIVATION.md#refinement), and where it is
   recorded in a_c its record is
   [AC-013](AXIOMATIC_CALCULUS.md#ac-013-transformation). The binding adds
   only which accounts the mapping joins and the evidence, in its
   execution environment, that discharges the preservation (P1, P0, P4a,
   P6).

Application in this method. The relation governs realisation at four
points. The Design rule (§2) places the choice of stack, human process or
combination in design, and that choice is the execution binding.
Ambiguity governance (§5) treats the choice as the step that narrows the
executable realisation class, so a major ambiguity about stack or
execution admissibility is recorded and governed there. A change to a
binding enters through intake triage and takes its change class (§4); a
change that needs a weaker obligation is a change to the WHAT at its
owning layer, never a tenant's choice. The steps of construction (§8) are
carried out under the binding of the tenant doing the work (P2, P6).

Development of several tenants. How a source project keeps its tenants'
work apart and merges it, including branches, working copies, territories,
review points and the merge rule, is that project's own law, bound in its
product definition as local axioms
([PRODUCT_DEFINITION §6](PRODUCT_DEFINITION.md#6-local-constitutional-binding))
or chosen in a tenant's design. This method prescribes none of these
mechanics. What it does prescribe for several tenants, the independence
of each tenant's ticket lifecycle and the review of each tenant's
tickets, is
[TICKETS §4](TICKETS.md#multi-build-tenant-independence) and
[§6 Multi-build-tenant review](TICKETS.md#multi-build-tenant-review)
(P6, P0).

Purpose and material relation: the same obligations can be realised by
different means, software, people or both. The tenant owns its choice of
means and the evidence for it while the WHAT keeps its meaning, so a
particular stack never becomes method machinery and a human or mixed
process needs no parallel method. The material relation is whether the
kind of executor, a person's participation, a tool's convenience or a
structural validation can change what satisfies an obligation, or grant
authority (P2, P1, P6). Two determinations conserve the predecessor's
constitutional chain (rc.2 #constitutional-chain): one WHAT realised by
one or more independent tenants whatever the layout, and tenant-local
realisation derivative until ratified (rule 1). Rule 4 applies by
reference the law of EVALUATION §6 that conforming tenants need not
behave identically outside the contract, which is new in that member.
The rest of this section is new in this corpus.

segments.heading: TICKETS
segments.text:
# TICKETS

Tier 2. Owns the work carriers of the method: goals, tickets, sprints,
comments and execution contracts as one model; the default layout and the
bindings that locate the carriers; the sprint rules; the ticket rules,
including triage-first intake, the change class the ticket records and the
upward propagation check; the selection of the smallest lawful carrier for
a piece of work and the carrier side of execution-contract admission; the
separation of execution from verification authority; the continuity of
recorded judgment and owner rulings; condition-based closure and reuse;
test case authority; the implementation-migration ticket category with its
declaration, checklist and review rules; one-truth state projection; the
recommended ticket and sprint shape; the operating mode. It is realised
from [FOUNDATIONS](FOUNDATIONS.md), [ACTIVATION](ACTIVATION.md) and
[EVALUATION](EVALUATION.md) and is the T area named by
[SPEC_METHOD §1](SPEC_METHOD.md#method-identity): nothing here is
foundational, every clause names the principle that requires it (P0 to P6,
FOUNDATIONS §3), and each mechanism could be realised differently under the
same principles. The change classes a ticket records are
[SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#change-classes), which is the triage target
of every clause here that names a class; the step side of admission is
[ACTIVATION §1](ACTIVATION.md#admission); the generic law of claims,
independent assessment and acceptance is EVALUATION §1, §3 and §5; the
testing law is ASSURANCE. This member defines none of those twice. Its
family table (F13) opens §5. A route
written `rc.2 #anchor` is into
`stdo://releases/v2.5.1-rc.2/standards/TICKET_METHOD.md` and is provenance
only; nothing here depends on that cut to be applied.

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers
segments.text: ## 1. Work carriers

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers/Goals
segments.text:
### Goals

The product definition's `ticketing.goals` binding locates the current epic
layer; `GOALS.md` is the default file (PRODUCT_DEFINITION §1). Goals are
broader than one ticket, narrower and more current than the intent surface,
and the place to state the active work wave and what matters now. Goals are
not the durable unit of execution tracking (P2, P3; rc.2 #goals).

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers/Ticket records
segments.text:
### Ticket records

Tickets are the enduring work records. Each ticket is one durable record,
one markdown file being the default carrier; the source of truth for that
unit of work; durable across sessions; and typed, so that bugs and features
share one system. A ticket is used when work needs independent durable
identity: feature work, bug tracking, spikes and chores (P3, P4b; rc.2
#tickets).

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers/Sprints
segments.text:
### Sprints

Sprints are bounded execution batches. Each sprint is one manifest under
the product definition's optional `ticketing.sprints.root` binding,
`.ai-workspace/sprints/` being the default; a control surface for a bounded
body of work; a place to batch repeated authority references, closure law,
evidence expectations and deferred local compliance debt; and closed by an
explicit sprint-close review. Sprints are not constitutional authority: they
operate under SPEC_METHOD and the project surfaces they cite
([SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#sprint-execution-boundary) states the
sprint boundary; this member states the mechanics) (P2, P6; rc.2 #sprints).

A sprint may contain durable tickets, manifest-local iteration entries, or
both. Tickets carry work items that need durable identity across sessions;
manifest-local iteration entries carry small changes whose only independent
value is traceability inside the sprint. The sprint is the batch authority;
it does not erase the need for paydown tickets when close review finds debt
that must survive past the sprint (P2, P4b).

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers/Comments
segments.text:
### Comments

The product definition's `ticketing.comments.root` binding is the message
board; `.ai-workspace/comments/` is the default. Comments are for publishing
ideas, strategy notes, reviews, handoffs, closure summaries, and decisions
with their reasoning. Comments are not task status authority. A comment
is a post of [POSTING_GUIDE](POSTING_GUIDE.md), which states what it
carries, its structure and its discussion state. A decision recorded in a
comment takes its authority from the surface that owns the decision, once
it is adopted there ([POSTING_GUIDE §9](POSTING_GUIDE.md#9-ratification)),
and has none of its own (P6, P3; rc.2 #comments).

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers/Execution contracts
segments.text:
### Execution contracts

Tickets are durable work authority. An execution contract is the run-scoped
admitted work surface derived from a ticket, from a sprint manifest plus an
included ticket or iteration entry, or drafted during intake when no durable
or sprint-local work identity is required. The three lifetimes differ: a
ticket survives sessions and work waves; a sprint survives one bounded
execution batch and its close review; an execution contract is the current
admitted execution function for one run. Execution contracts are not a
rival backlog or a second planning surface (P0, P3; rc.2
#execution-contracts).

They exist so that the system can classify the work before execution; admit
or reject the drafted classification against deterministic criteria; log
the admitted execution basis into runtime and event truth; assemble prompts
from admitted work law instead of from raw user phrasing; and evaluate
closure against the same admitted criteria. The intended loop: work
arrives; the system selects the smallest lawful work carrier for its
required lifetime (§5); an agent drafts one run-scoped execution contract
from that carrier; the system validates and admits or rejects the contract
(ACTIVATION §1, Admission); execution may proceed in the same invocation
under the admitted contract; closure is checked against that same contract;
the resulting state still flows through normal proof, gap analysis and
repricing (P6, P2).

segments.heading: TICKETS/1. Work carriers/Milestones and phase-scoped truth (UP-006)
segments.text:
### Milestones and phase-scoped truth (UP-006)

A ticket may contain several closure-bearing milestones without becoming
several tickets. Each milestone has stable identity, a bounded claim,
relevant dependencies, current state, required evidence, and an explicit
relation to ticket closure (P3; rc.2
#milestone-and-phase-scoped-truth-stdo-up-006).

Milestone acceptance proves only its declared claim. Accepted design does
not satisfy implementation, installed proof, qualification or release.
Ticket completion requires every closure-bearing milestone to be accepted;
optional or deferred work requires an explicit disposition and owner. Each
milestone is a work claim under §7 Condition-based closure and reuse, so
its acceptance follows that condition for its own declared claim, and a
ticket is complete only when the condition holds for each of them.
Commentary and generated summaries cannot mutate milestone or ticket truth
(P6, P4b).

segments.heading: TICKETS/2. Layout and authority
segments.text: ## 2. Layout and authority

segments.heading: TICKETS/2. Layout and authority/Default layout
segments.text:
### Default layout

The starter file layout (P2, P3; rc.2 #default-layout):

```text
stdo_default.json

specification/
├── GOALS.md

.ai-workspace/
├── sprints/
├── tickets/
│   ├── backlog/
│   ├── active/
│   └── completed/
└── comments/
    └── <agent-id>/
```

The applicable product definition resolves POSTING_GUIDE and this member
from its exact shared installed basis (PRODUCT_DEFINITION §4); their
absence from the project tree is not absence from the governing method. A
conforming `stdo_<label>.json` definition may bind the same ticket, comment
and sprint roles to existing directories, repository resources, tracker
collections, API endpoints or product-scoped queries without restructuring
the project (PRODUCT_DEFINITION §1).

segments.heading: TICKETS/2. Layout and authority/Bindings and projections
segments.text:
### Bindings and projections

The bindings (P6, P3; rc.2 #authority): `ticketing.goals` locates the epic
layer; `ticketing.sprints.root`, when present, is the bounded
execution-batch and sprint-close review layer;
`ticketing.tickets.lanes.backlog`, `.active` and `.completed` locate the
ticket authority; `ticketing.comments.root` locates the discussion and
publication layer. The paths of the default layout are the bindings
supplied by `stdo_default.json`. The definition locates these carriers and
does not own their ticket or comment content.

There is no separate mandatory `ACTIVE_TASKS.md` in this model. A project
that wants a board view may generate one from the bound ticket authority;
that board is a projection only and does not become the source of truth
unless the product definition explicitly rebinds the ticket authority to
that carrier and no rival remains (§7).

segments.heading: TICKETS/2. Layout and authority/Carrier substitution
segments.text:
### Carrier substitution

The durable local-file model is the default and remains valid whenever it
is selected. Another carrier is not required to reproduce its folders, but
it preserves the same ticket authority and refusal laws (§3 and §4, one
durable record). Growth the model admits includes a generated active board,
ticket dependency checks, links from tickets to scenario, requirement or
ADR surfaces, external sync with a real ticketing system, and message-board
integration through a standard tool-protocol capability. Under the bindings
above, a generated board is a projection, and a tracker that holds tickets
is lawful only as an explicit rebinding of the ticket authority by the
product definition with no rival surface remaining, so neither growth
changes the authority or refusal laws (P2, P6; rc.2 #future-extensions).

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules
segments.text: ## 3. Sprint rules

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules/One durable record per sprint
segments.text:
### One durable record per sprint

Each sprint has one durable manifest record; the default carrier is one
markdown file. Another bound carrier preserves the same identity, required
fields, history, closure law and one-truth relation (P3, P4b; rc.2
#one-durable-record-per-sprint). For a local file, the filename should
carry a stable id and a short slug. Recommended local-file naming:
`SPRINT-2026-04-30-process-navigator.md` and
`SPRINT-2026-05-12-dashboard-density.md`.

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules/Manifest fields
segments.text:
### Manifest fields

Each sprint manifest records at least `id`, `title`, `status`, `goal`,
`opened_at`, `updated_at`, `authority_refs`, `scope`, `excluded_boundaries`,
`expected_change_classes`, `included_tickets` or `iterations`,
`closure_trigger`, `closure_law`, `proof_surface`, `deferred_compliance`,
`non_closure_conditions` and `paydown_policy` (P4b, P2; rc.2
#sprint-manifest-required-fields).

`authority_refs` names the upstream goals, intent, product, requirement,
design or other governing surfaces the sprint operates under.
`excluded_boundaries` names what the sprint is not allowed to change;
typical exclusions are product truth, data contracts, runtime semantics,
governance and closure law, public carrier shape and release criteria.
`deferred_compliance` names any local proof, review, accessibility,
screenshot, walkthrough, test, design wording or trace cleanup
intentionally deferred until sprint close. `paydown_policy` states how
deferred debt becomes accepted, ticketed, repriced or removed during close
review (P6).

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules/Sprint status
segments.text:
### Sprint status

The minimum sprint status model is `active`, `closing`, `closed` and
`superseded` (P5, P3; rc.2 #sprint-status). `active`: iteration is admitted
inside the sprint boundary. `closing`: new iteration is frozen while close
review and paydown classification run. `closed`: close review finished and
all remaining debt is accepted, ticketed, repriced or removed.
`superseded`: the sprint boundary was wrong and a new authority surface,
sprint or ticket set replaced it. A project may add `planned` or
`cancelled`; those states do not replace close review.

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules/Sprint admission
segments.text:
### Sprint admission

A sprint may admit work only when the manifest makes the boundary
reviewable. Admission requires a bounded scope, cited authority, expected
change classes, explicit excluded boundaries, a closure law, non-closure
conditions, and a paydown policy for deferred compliance (P6, P2; rc.2
#sprint-admission).

The sprint may batch repeated closure criteria that would otherwise be
copied into every included ticket. It may not batch away intake triage:
substantive included tickets still record their lawful `change_class` and
`re_entry_point` (§4, Triage metadata). Manifest-local iteration entries
may rely on the sprint's declared class only while they remain inside the
sprint scope and excluded boundaries (P4b).

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules/Compliance escrow
segments.text:
### Compliance escrow

A sprint may defer local compliance proof only when the manifest names the
deferred proof or cleanup class; the debt is local to the sprint's admitted
surface; the expected correction cost is lower than the per-change proof
cost; the sprint is short enough that the debt remains reviewable; and the
close review classifies and pays down the debt. Deferred compliance is not
silent debt: it is escrow held by the sprint, and
[SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#sprint-execution-boundary) states that
escrow satisfies no method, release or product closure until paid down,
accepted or repriced (P2, P4b, P6; rc.2 #sprint-compliance-escrow).

The following may be eligible for escrow when the governing method allows
it: screenshots or
walkthrough capture; visual review; accessibility cleanup; replay proof for
product-meaningful user-interface interactions; design wording cleanup; trace cleanup;
local realisation cleanup. The following may not be hidden in escrow: new
product truth; new
or changed data contracts; new runtime, governance, closure, provenance or
evidence semantics; missing constructive carriers; changed public
published-function or public carrier contracts; law-changing work that
needs `goal_reprice`, `intent_reprice`, `product_reprice`,
`requirement_reprice` or `design_reframe`. If one of those appears during
the sprint, the sprint records the finding and the work exits the sprint
path through a standalone ticket, a repricing action or sprint supersession
(P6).

segments.heading: TICKETS/3. Sprint rules/Close review
segments.text:
### Close review

Sprint close begins by moving the manifest to `status: closing`. While
closing: new iteration inside that sprint is frozen; every included ticket
or iteration entry is reviewed against the manifest; accumulated evidence
is checked for durability; changed surfaces are walked against cited
authority; deferred compliance is classified; paydown tickets are opened
where debt must survive past the close review (P6, P4b; rc.2
#sprint-close-review).

Each reviewed item is classified as one of `accepted` (compliant under the
sprint authority), `local_paydown` (local debt remains and is captured by a
paydown ticket), `design_reframe` (the work needs design repricing),
`requirement_reprice` (the work needs requirement repricing),
`product_reprice` (the work changes product definition) or `remove` (the
work should be backed out or kept out of closure) (P5). A sprint may move to
`closed` only when every item and every debt entry is classified and the
resulting paydown or repricing work is durable. Sprint close can accept
local paydown debt only when the governing method allows that debt to
survive as explicit follow-up; it cannot accept hidden authority drift
(P6).

Close classifications and the core. A close classification is the
outcome of close review for one reviewed item, made against the sprint
authority the manifest cites; the close review must classify, under that
authority. The classification uses
[ACTIVATION §3 Disposition](ACTIVATION.md#disposition) only for its
result mapping: the candidate is the reviewed item, its boundary is the
sprint's close under the cited authority, and the classification consumes
the core results of the item's review and stays separate from them, as
acceptance stays separate from assessment
([FOUNDATIONS §4 Results](FOUNDATIONS.md#results)). Each classification
takes exactly one core value, for the predicate "the reviewed item is
accepted as compliant under the sprint authority", and the table names
the disposition whose condition it matches, where one does (P5, P6):

| Classification | Matching disposition | Core value | Ground, and how it narrows or differs from the disposition's condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| `accepted` | `accept` | satisfied | the item is compliant under the sprint authority |
| `local_paydown` | `local_repair` | falsified | local debt remains and is captured by a paydown ticket; the debt is the counterexample. The governing relation stays coherent, because an item whose governing authority must change takes a repricing classification instead. It differs from `local_repair` in where the repair is carried: by the paydown ticket, which survives the close where the method allows that debt to survive |
| `design_reframe` | `re_enter` | invalid_basis | the accepted design that governs the item must change, so the authority the sprint cites cannot support accepting it |
| `requirement_reprice` | `re_enter` | invalid_basis | a governing requirement must change, with the same consequence |
| `product_reprice` | `re_enter` | invalid_basis | the work changes the product definition, which the authority the sprint cites cannot support |
| `remove` | none | falsified | the work is backed out or kept out of closure; the reason for removal is the counterexample. No disposition of ACTIVATION §3 has this condition, because removal does not require a violated governing relation or a competing truth path |

The layer that `design_reframe`, `requirement_reprice` and
`product_reprice` name is a declared fact, not a further result: it is
the change class of [SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#change-classes) at
which the work re-enters, and it travels with the core value as the
domain outcome (FOUNDATIONS §4 Results, Recording). The outcome of a
debt entry, accepted, ticketed, repriced or removed (Sprint status,
`closed`), is likewise classified by the close review and mapped at the
close boundary, for the predicate "the debt entry is accepted under the
sprint authority": accepted matches `accept` (`satisfied`), ticketed
matches `local_repair` (`falsified`), removed takes `falsified` with no
matching disposition, and repriced matches `re_enter`
(`invalid_basis`), on the grounds of `accepted`, `local_paydown`,
`remove` and the repricing classifications respectively. The mappings
add no disposition and no core value. The condition for `closed`
above requires an outcome for every item and debt entry, not a
`satisfied` one. The mappings are new in this corpus.
Purpose and material relation: a consumer that combines close outcomes
with other results cannot read remaining debt, needed repricing or
removal as compliance (P5, P6).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules
segments.text: ## 4. Ticket rules

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/One durable record per ticket
segments.text:
### One durable record per ticket

Each ticket has one durable authoritative record; the default carrier is
one markdown file. A repository or external tracker carrier is lawful only
when it preserves the required ticket contract, history, state transition,
stable identity, searchability and closure semantics without a co-equal
local copy (P3, P4b; rc.2 #one-durable-record-per-ticket). For a local
file, the filename should carry a stable id and a short slug. Recommended
local-file naming:
`T-001-add-product-layer.md`, `B-002-fix-reset-manifest-id.md`,
`S-003-evaluate-integration-capability.md`,
`C-004-clean-up-trace-tags.md`.

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Multi-build-tenant independence
segments.text:
### Multi-build-tenant independence

This clause consumes the build-tenancy bounded context
`urn:stdo:bounded-context:build-tenancy` declared by PRODUCT_DEFINITION §8.
This member owns the multi-build-tenant work-item and ticket-lifecycle
relation inside that context; it does not redefine build-tenant identity or
realisation meaning (P3, P1; rc.2 #multi-build-tenant-ticket-independence).

A multi-build-tenant work item is one admitted upstream work item with more
than one build-tenant execution line. The upstream authority and each
tenant-local ticket retain distinct identities and lifecycles. If one
source, product or design work item must be realised in more than one build
tenant, its tenant realisations are not tracked inside one ticket
lifecycle. The rule governs backlog and active tickets; it is not
retroactive for completed tickets unless a completed ticket is reopened or
explicitly repriced. It does not make every ticket multi-tenant: tenant
duplication is used only when the same admitted work item genuinely has
more than one tenant execution line (P3).

The three lawful cases: an upstream-only ticket (source, product or design
authority only; no tenant duplicate yet); a single-tenant ticket (one
tenant-local execution line; no sibling duplicate required); a multi-tenant
work item (one upstream authority ticket and one suffixed tenant-local
ticket per tenant execution line). For the multi-tenant case: keep the
upstream source, product or design ticket as its own authority surface;
duplicate the work item into one tenant-local ticket per build tenant;
append a build-tenant mnemonic to the base ticket id and filename; keep
status, proof, closure and reopen logic independent for each tenant.
Recommended examples: `B-030-publish-capability-profile...` as the
source ticket,
`B-030-T1-publish-capability-profile...` and
`B-030-T2-publish-capability-profile...` as the tenant tickets.

The law: one ticket does not claim closure for more than one build-tenant
lifecycle; a tenant-local blocker or false closure in one tenant is not
hidden by green status in another; tenant-local proof, repricing and
reopening remain tenant-local (P3, P6). If a tenant-local duplicate
exists, it should record `source_ticket` and `build_tenant`. The
`build_tenant` value identifies the
applicable entry in the product's `how.build_tenants` definition; a path
name, display alias or tracker label does not replace that identity unless
the product definition binds it as the identity. The unsuffixed base ticket
may remain the upstream product or design authority. If the work item is
multi-tenant, tenant execution and closure for backlog and active work live
on the suffixed duplicates; if it is single-tenant, no sibling duplicate is
required.

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Required fields
segments.text:
### Required fields

Each ticket records at least `id`, `title`, `type`, `ticket_category`,
`status`, `goal`, `change_intent`, `change_class`, `re_entry_point`,
`triaged_at`, `created_at` and `updated_at` (P4b, P3; rc.2
#required-fields). Recommended additional fields: `priority`,
`dependencies`, `links`, `intake_source`, `affected_boundary`,
`source_ticket` when the ticket duplicates or derives from another ticket,
and `build_tenant` when the ticket is tenant-local.

For `ticket_category: implementation_migration` the ticket also carries
`migration_strategy` and `library_usage`; `governing_library` when
`library_usage` is `consume` or `extend`; and `library_rationale` when
`library_usage` is `none` (§6). A tenant-local implementation migration
also carries `build_tenant`, and `source_ticket` when it duplicates or
derives from an upstream source, product or design ticket.

For execution-contract admission the runtime-drafted contract should also
carry, at minimum, `target_truth`, `superseded_truth` when relevant,
`closure_law`, `evaluation_criteria`, `non_closure_conditions` and
`proof_surface` (§5).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Types
segments.text:
### Types

The minimum common set of ticket types is `feature`, `bug`, `spike` and
`chore`. A project may add more; the default set should be enough for
most cases
(P3; rc.2 #allowed-types).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Category
segments.text:
### Category

Ticket category is orthogonal to ticket type: type answers what kind of
work record this is; category answers what execution or migration
discipline governs the ticket (P3, P1; rc.2 #ticket-category). The minimum
common set is `ordinary` and `implementation_migration`, so a `feature`,
`bug`, `spike` or `chore` may carry either. `implementation_migration` is
used when the ticket is not "change code until tests pass" but a governed
replacement of one implementation truth path with another across producers,
consumers, projections and proof surfaces: a bug ticket that replaces an old
tracker or read-model family with one new authoritative carrier; a feature
ticket that introduces a new public interface and requires every producer
and consumer to migrate before closure; a refactor ticket that removes a
bridge path or compatibility facade from an authoritative contract family.

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Inside-out sequencing
segments.text:
### Inside-out sequencing

For `ticket_category: implementation_migration`, ticket sequencing reflects
the inside-out rule of
[SPEC_METHOD §7](SPEC_METHOD.md#inside-out-first-sequencing) (P4b, P6;
rc.2 #inside-out-first-ticket-sequencing). Tickets that publish or admit
the new authoritative source carrier are the upstream tickets in the wave.
Tickets that harden prompt assembly, projections, reports, dossiers, review
surfaces or other downstream consumers depend on those upstream source
tickets. A downstream ticket may carry exploratory work while the source
ticket is active, but that work is non-closure evidence until the source
carrier is admitted and authoritative. A downstream ticket does not close
while its upstream source-carrier ticket remains open. When one migration
wave introduces a new source carrier and then its prompt, projection or
read-model consumers, the dependency chain runs `source carrier ->
downstream consumers`, never the reverse.

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Change class
segments.text:
### Change class

Ticket type and change class are orthogonal: type answers what kind of
work record this is; change class answers where the change lawfully
re-enters the constitutional chain. A ticket records the `change_class`
declared by intake triage, using the classes of
[SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#change-classes) (P4b, P2; rc.2
#change-class).

Common pairings: `feature` with `goal_reprice`, `intent_reprice`,
`product_reprice`, `requirement_reprice` or `design_reframe`; `bug` with
`requirement_reprice`, `design_reframe` or `realization_refactor`; `chore`
with `design_reframe` or `realization_refactor`; `spike` as exploratory
work that still carries the current triage class and should terminate
either in a more specific downstream ticket or in an explicit decision
that no further substantive change is required.

Ticket category and change class are also orthogonal: `change_class`
governs lawful constitutional re-entry; `ticket_category` governs ticket
execution and closure discipline. A ticket may therefore be `type: bug`,
`ticket_category: implementation_migration`, `change_class: design_reframe`
without contradiction (P3).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Upward propagation check
segments.text:
### Upward propagation check

Triage consumes the computed classification of
[SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#computed-classification-and-treatment) for
the declared owner and layer traversal, the complete relevant public
membership and value delta, the accepted-design scope and trace coverage,
and the rule-determined treatment. The owning work carrier references that
exact result and its residuals; a new role does not repeat an unchanged
walk (P4b, P2; rc.2 #upward-propagation-check).

Before declaring `realization_refactor` for a bug, establish that the
current requirement and the accepted realising design govern the affected
behaviour and remain sufficient for the authorised outcome. Their presence
proves no coverage. Missing or ambiguous evidence leaves the affected
treatment unknown; it is not proof that the governing layer itself is
absent (P6).

The re-entry rule is SPEC_METHOD §4's: the
[change classes](SPEC_METHOD.md#change-classes) with their re-entry
points, and the smallest lawful re-entry that step 4 of
[Computed classification and treatment](SPEC_METHOD.md#computed-classification-and-treatment)
exposes, with the paragraph after the four steps: a candidate's public
violation does not select a new contract, and the governing owner is
re-entered only for an explicitly changed desired outcome or an
established governing insufficiency. For a bug, this check
refines that rule into an upward walk from the realised surface that
checks each layer and stops at the highest layer found missing or
insufficient for the authorised outcome, and the class is the one that
re-enters there:

| Where the walk stops | Change class | Action |
|---|---|---|
| the governing requirement is missing or insufficient | `requirement_reprice` | re-enter the requirement's owner |
| the requirement is sufficient, and the realising design is missing or insufficient | `design_reframe` | re-enter Design |
| an actual upstream Goal, Intent or Product change | `goal_reprice`, `intent_reprice` or `product_reprice` | follow the change to its owner rather than stopping at a familiar file |
| the current requirement and accepted design suffice, and the implementation deviates | `realization_refactor` | repair or reject the candidate |

Unresolved meaning remains J and a reserved choice remains O, as that
paragraph states (P2, P6).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Triage metadata
segments.text:
### Triage metadata

Because tickets are the durable authority surface for work tracking, a
ticket for substantive work carries the minimum metadata required by the
intake triage of [SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#universal-intake-triage):
the declared `change_intent`, the lawful `change_class`, the lawful
`re_entry_point`, and when triage occurred in `triaged_at` (P4b, P2; rc.2
#triage-metadata). The recorded values are those intake triage declared
(Change class and Upward propagation check above).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Status
segments.text:
### Status

The minimum ticket status model is `backlog`, `active` and `completed`. A
project may add `blocked`, `cancelled` or other explicit local states; the
base method starts with the three (P5, P3; rc.2 #allowed-status).

The ticket statuses, any local state a project adds, the lanes below, the
sprint statuses of §3 and the `migration_strategy` and `library_usage`
values of §6 are declared states of their carriers, not results, and map
to no core value; the recorded `change_class` is a declared state under
[SPEC_METHOD §4](SPEC_METHOD.md#change-classes). The close
classifications and debt-entry outcomes of §3
Close review are results, mapped there. An evaluation that reads a
declared state returns its own core value with its predicate under
[FOUNDATIONS §4 Results](FOUNDATIONS.md#results). Purpose and material
relation: a declared state is never combined as an evaluation result, so
a ticket marked `completed`, or a sprint marked `closed`, cannot stand in
for a `satisfied` result (P5, P1).

segments.heading: TICKETS/4. Ticket rules/Lanes
segments.text:
### Lanes

Backlog tickets live at the product definition's
`ticketing.tickets.lanes.backlog` binding, by default
`.ai-workspace/tickets/backlog/`; active tickets at
`ticketing.tickets.lanes.active`, by default `.ai-workspace/tickets/active/`;
completed tickets move to `ticketing.tickets.lanes.completed`, by default
`.ai-workspace/tickets/completed/` (P0, P3; rc.2 #ticket-lanes). `backlog`
is accepted durable work that should remain visible but is not part of the
current execution focus; `active` is the current bounded execution set;
`completed` is closed work retained as history. The lanes keep the live
execution set small enough that `rg` remains fast and readable without
forcing deferred work into comments or goals.

segments.heading: TICKETS/5. From carrier to execution
segments.text:
## 5. From carrier to execution

If a derived surface or projected frame of this member is insufficient,
the actor reads this member only for the named unresolved lifecycle or
proof question and cites the clauses used (P2, P6; provenance rc.2
authority_compressions/ticket_method.compressed.md, a claim no rc.2 body
states; prompt construction is
[ACTIVATION §2](ACTIVATION.md#2-context-construction-under-an-envelope)).

segments.heading: TICKETS/5. From carrier to execution/Foundation to law: work carriers
segments.text:
### Foundation to law: work carriers

This family (F13 in the index of
[FOUNDATIONS §3 Foundation to law](FOUNDATIONS.md#foundation-to-law))
decides which record carries a piece of work, what that record may claim
and when the work closes. Its instance premises, which the commitments do
not supply, are named in the rows as follows: lifetimes, work and its
obligations last one run, one bounded batch or longer; several surfaces,
goals, tickets, comments, boards and summaries can each appear to state
the same work state; several tenants, one work item may be realised in
more than one build tenant; migrations, some work replaces one
authoritative truth path with another across producers, consumers and
proofs; carriers vary, a project may keep its carriers in files, trackers
or services. Each commitment's standing is written as the table of
commitments in FOUNDATIONS §3 states it.

| Premises, with standing | Consequence that follows | Rule in this member that states it | Added domain or policy choice, and its owner | Pillar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P4b (derived from P0 and P2, with P0's premise that step-produced facts are not re-acquirable); P3 (independent); P2 (independent); P6 (independent); P0 (recovered); instance: lifetimes | By P0 an actor's context does not outlive its run, and by P4b a step-produced fact that is not recorded is lost, so an obligation that must outlive the run is recorded on a carrier whose lifetime covers it before the run returns. By P2 nothing is added that the outcome does not need, so every execution runs under one run-scoped contract drawn from the smallest such carrier (an admitted ticket, a sprint entry or the run itself), and a durable ticket is created only for state that must survive; by P6 creating one needs ticket-state authority. | [Carrier selection](#carrier-selection); §1 [Goals](#goals), [Ticket records](#ticket-records), [Execution contracts](#execution-contracts) | the carrier kinds and the selection table, which apply this order to named lifetimes: a policy of this member; where each carrier lives: the product definition ([PRODUCT_DEFINITION §8](PRODUCT_DEFINITION.md#8-what-how-and-work-carriers)) | 1, 8, 9 |
| P6 (independent); P2 (independent); P4b (derived from P0 and P2, with P0's premise that step-produced facts are not re-acquirable); P3 (independent); instance: lifetimes | By P6 work needs an admitted authority, and a record's presence or prose creates none, so work executes only under admitted upstream work authority, and a carrier's presence, lane, status or prose is neither the admission of a contract nor the admission of a growth basis.
